title: Which four questions decide whether a client should enter a new market?
description: "Should the client enter this market?" A new country, customer segment or product category.
hook: Four questions decide whether a client should enter a new market: is the market attractive, can the client win, will it pay back the investment, and can the client actually pull it off. The arithmetic underneath is simple: the prize is market size × the share you can win × margin, compared with what it costs to get in. Here is the structure, how to adapt it, and a short worked example.
body:
When you will use it

Use it when a client is considering a new country, a new customer segment or a new product category, and the question is whether to go in. It is a decide question: you test the idea against a few yes-or-no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear answer and the conditions attached. See which framework to use for each type of question for the other families.

Ask this first

Why this market, and what would success look like, by when? Is there a payback or return target?

Without a target, you cannot say whether eight years to pay back is good or bad. With one, your recommendation has a yardstick.

The structure

  • Is the market attractive?
    • Size and growth
    • Typical margins
    • Barriers to entry
  • Can we win?
    • Competitors and their strength
    • What customers need
    • Our edge
  • Will it pay?
    • Revenue we can expect
    • Running costs
    • Upfront investment, compared with the payback target
  • Can we pull it off?
    • Capabilities we lack, which decides whether to build, partner or buy
    • Timing and a pilot
    • Key risks

Make it your own

The questions run in order, and each can stop the analysis: a small, low-margin market makes "can we win?" irrelevant. Tailor the branches to the client. For a retailer, "will it pay?" is the economics of one store multiplied up. For a software firm, it is customers won × revenue per customer against the cost of a local sales team. And remember that "enter" is not one decision: owning, franchising, partnering and acquiring a local player have very different costs, speed and control. The build, partner or buy tip compares them.

A short worked example

A bakery-café chain is considering 20 stores in a new city of about 1 million people. Each store costs $400k to open. The figures are illustrative.

Will one store pay? Expect 400 purchases a day at $5, over 350 trading days:

  • Revenue: 400 × $5 × 350 = $700k a year
  • Ingredients and packaging at 30%: $210k
  • Rent, staff and other store costs: $350k, mostly fixed
  • Store contribution: $700k − $210k − $350k = $140k a year

Will 20 stores pay? Upfront: 20 × $400k = $8M. Contribution: 20 × $140k = $2.8M, minus about $0.6M of local management and marketing, leaves $2.2M a year. Payback: $8M ÷ $2.2M ≈ 3.6 years, before ramp-up.

Is the demand credible? 20 stores × 400 purchases = 8,000 a day, under 1% of the city's population. That seems reasonable, but check footfall at likely sites and how busy rivals are.

Stress-test the key assumption. Because most store costs are fixed, profit is very sensitive to traffic. At 300 purchases a day, revenue falls to $525k, and contribution to $525k − $157.5k − $350k = $17.5k per store. Across 20 stores that is $350k, less than the $600k of local overhead, so the city loses money. A 25% shortfall in traffic turns a 3.6-year payback into a loss. Our explainer on operating leverage shows why.

Recommendation: enter, but in stages. Open three to five stores, measure daily transactions and repeat visits over a few months, and commit to the rest only if traffic is near 400 a day. Consider franchising some sites to cut the upfront cost.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer describes:

The city has a growing café culture and young professionals, so there's a big opportunity, though competition is strong.

A strong answer quantifies and finds the swing factor:

At 400 purchases a day each store makes $140k and the rollout pays back in under four years. But at 300 a day the city loses money, so I'd pilot a handful of stores before committing $8M.

The mistakes to avoid

  1. Never comparing the prize with the cost of getting in. The investment and payback usually decide the case.
  2. Assuming a share or volume without checking it. Sense-check from the bottom up.
  3. Ignoring the route in. Owning, franchising and partnering change the economics.
  4. Giving a bare yes or no. Say how to enter and how to limit the downside.

Practise with real prompts

1. Should a luxury hotel group launch a budget hotel brand?

Show the answer
  • Market: size and growth of budget hotels; competitors and their returns.
  • Economics: cost to build or convert, room rates, occupancy; return against the cost of capital.
  • Fit and risk: can a luxury operator run low-cost hotels well? Damage to the luxury brand.
  • Cannibalisation: guests who would trade down from the group's own hotels.

Where to start: economics per hotel. If one hotel does not make money, nothing else matters.

The trap: forgetting brand risk and cannibalisation.

2. Should a coffee chain sell its beans in supermarkets?

Show the answer
  • Market: size of premium coffee in supermarkets; competitors and shelf space.
  • Economics: price, the retailer's margin, our cost; volume needed to pay back.
  • Cannibalisation and halo: café visits lost against new customers and awareness gained.
  • Brand and operations: a premium image next to discounts; roasting capacity.

Where to start: net profit after the café visits we might lose.

The trap: ignoring the effect on café visits and the brand.

3. Should an airline launch a daily London to Lagos route?

Show the answer
  • Demand: business travellers, people visiting family, cargo; seasonality.
  • Competition: rivals' flights, prices and loyalty schemes; their likely response.
  • Economics: revenue per flight against cost per flight.
  • Risks: currency and getting cash out; airport slots and approvals.

Where to start: profit per flight compared with what the aircraft earns on its current route.

The trap: forgetting the opportunity cost of the aircraft.
